newsitem.title: FRANCE: French ex-PM says Jospin spends more, risks euro.
newsitem.headline: French ex-PM says Jospin spends more, risks euro.

text.p: Former conservative prime minister Edouard Balladur accused the new Socialist-led government on Friday of planning spending increases that could derail France's plans to join a single European currency.

The government reiterated that France was committed to the euro from 1999 after Prime Minister Lionel Jospin outlined his plans including the creation of 700,000 jobs and cuts in the working week to 35 hours in a keynote speech to parliament on Thursday.

French media gave Jospin good marks for honesty in making a start on campaign promises but noted he put off budget choices until autumn. A cartoon in the daily Le Monde showed Jospin in a rubber ring telling parliament: "See you in September".
Trade union leaders faulted Jospin for raising the minimum wage by only four percent.

Balladur, who was premier in 1993-95, said Jospin's "Pink-Green-Red" coalition including Socialists, Greens and Communists would raise spending by "a good 50 billion francs" ($8.6 billion) a year with policies including wage rises and higher "back-to-school" payments to families.
Balladur's figure was more than double the initial estimates by private economists of the cost of the main measures. And Jospin announced cuts in child benefits for better-off families.
"I didn't hear...any talk of reducing public spending," Balladur told Europe 1 radio. "On the contrary, it is going to be raised. That's not the way to revive growth."

"France has a big interest in entering Europe and building the single currency," Balladur added. "In the current state of things, if spending is raised, if our social system is made rigid still further, I don't see how we will be able to stick to our European ambitions."
France needs to cut its deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997 to qualify for the euro from 1999. In 1996, it was 4.2 percent.
Employment Minister Martine Aubry, Jospin's number two, insisted there was no contradiction between Jospin's spending plans and his intention to bring France into the euro.
"The fiscal and social reform will indeed allow the country to stay on track" for the euro, she told RTL radio.
"Everything is urgent," said Aubry, the daughter of former European Commission president Jacques Delors. "But the most urgent thing is jobs."
Jospin, who has said he will not impose extra austerity to qualify for the euro, said first signs were that public finances were "serious". A full audit would be completed in mid-July.
French markets were little changed on Friday. The CAC stock index was up 0.5 percent, recouping a similar fall on Thursday.

Jospin won unusual praise on Friday from a senior conservative opponent for standing up to German Chancellor Helmut Kohl with his stress on jobs to match a German-championed plan to limit budget deficits under the euro.

Former interior minister Charles Pasqua, a senior member of the Gaullist party founded by President Jacques Chirac, criticised both Chirac and Gaullist ex-prime minister Alain Juppe for failing to confront Germany at times of tension.
Jospin "has proven that we don't have to accept the German position as sacrosanct," Pasqua told France Inter radio. "We don't have to accept what Kohl says as the law of the prophets."
Jospin said that he would stick to all his campaign promises but said it would require "time and perseverance".

"Lionel Jospin is socialist and intelligent. Not really cynical," the conservative daily Le Figaro wrote in an editorial. "However, he will need a lot of skill to reconcile what cannot be reconciled."
Le Parisien said in a front page headline "Jospin announced what he promised" -- as if that were unusual in French politics.
